Java vs TypeScript/JavaScript

Two Auth Services. Same Security Problem. Different Fighting Styles.

This page compares the Java Spring Boot implementation with the TypeScript/JavaScript NestJS implementation. The Java version is the mechanics-first build: persistent MongoDB storage, explicit BCrypt use, a hand-built HS256 JWT, form-based endpoints, and centralized Spring exception handling. The TypeScript/JavaScript version is the more complete Node-side implementation: DTO validation, JSON request bodies, bcrypt, access and refresh tokens, Swagger documentation, a health endpoint, safer logging, and Jest tests.

Compare the implementations Compare the code
Java advantage Real MongoDB persistence
Shared strength BCrypt password hashing
TypeScript advantage Refresh-token workflow
TypeScript advantage Swagger + Jest + DTO validation
Major similarities

The two implementations agree on the important security fundamentals

The frameworks and syntax are different, but the core security model is remarkably similar. Students should recognize these as the stable concepts that survive a language change.

Passwords are hashed

Java uses BCryptPasswordEncoder. TypeScript uses the bcrypt library. Neither implementation stores the submitted password as plain text.

Successful login issues a JWT

Both services issue an HS256 access token after a successful password check. The downstream service can use the signed token instead of receiving the password on every request.

Identity and roles go into claims

Both implementations carry the username as identity information and carry role or scope data so protected services can make authorization decisions.

Bad credentials become 401-style failures

Java throws a Spring ResponseStatusException. NestJS throws UnauthorizedException. Different framework mechanism, same HTTP-level intent.

Duplicate users are rejected

Java turns Mongo duplicate-key errors into conflict responses. NestJS checks the in-memory map and throws a ConflictException.

Controller delegates to service

Both implementations keep request routing separate from authentication logic. The controller accepts the request and hands the real work to an auth service.

The ring changes. The fundamentals do not. Whether the service is written in Java or TypeScript, the same questions remain: how are credentials stored, how are passwords checked, what claims go into the token, how long does the token live, and how does the API reject invalid input?
Key differences

Where the two implementations take different approaches

This is where the comparison gets useful. The differences are not merely syntax differences. Several of them change persistence, API design, token lifecycle, observability, or testability.

Java Spring Boot

Mechanics-first
Persistent users in MongoDB

UserAccount is a real Mongo document and UserAccountRepository extends MongoRepository. The service survives process restarts because the users are not kept only in memory.

Manual JWT construction

The Java implementation manually base64url-encodes the claims and manually creates the HMAC-SHA256 signature. This is excellent for understanding exactly what a JWT contains.

Richer current claim set

The Java token includes iss, aud, sub, scope, iat, and exp. Its access token lifetime is currently 24 hours.

Form-urlencoded endpoints

The controller accepts username and password as request parameters. This is simple to test but less expressive than a typed JSON DTO contract.

Central exception advice

App.java maps multiple exception types into structured ProblemDetail responses and adds the request path to the error payload.

Refresh token field exists, flow does not

The model has refreshTokenHash, but the supplied Java AuthService currently issues only an access token.

TypeScript/JavaScript NestJS

Feature-complete
Users are currently in memory

The NestJS service stores users in a Map<string, StoredUser>. That keeps the example compact, but users disappear when the process restarts.

Library-based JWT creation

jsonwebtoken.sign() handles the token assembly and signing. That is concise and typical of application code, but it hides the low-level JWT construction students can see explicitly in Java.

Shorter access token

The access token contains sub and roles and expires after 15 minutes. The short lifetime pairs naturally with the refresh-token flow.

JSON DTOs and runtime validation

RegisterDto and LoginDto define the incoming shapes, while a global ValidationPipe whitelists declared properties and rejects extras.

Refresh tokens are implemented

Login returns both an access token and a random 32-byte refresh token. refresh() can then issue a new access token without rechecking the password.

Swagger, health check, logger, Jest

The NestJS implementation includes API documentation, a readiness endpoint, a logging helper that cannot accept passwords or tokens, and tests that verify token claims.

QUIZ ALERT: access token vs refresh token

The access token is the credential sent to protected APIs. The refresh token is a separate, longer-lived credential used to obtain a new access token. The TypeScript implementation demonstrates that split directly; the Java model hints at it but does not complete the flow yet.

Detailed comparison matrix

One table for the whole matchup

This table is designed for classroom projection. Each row answers one concrete architecture question.

Area Java Spring Boot TypeScript/JavaScript NestJS Teaching takeaway
Framework Spring Boot NestJS on Node.js Both use dependency injection and controller/service separation.
User storage MongoDB through Spring Data In-memory Map Java is persistent today; NestJS is intentionally simpler today.
Password hashing BCryptPasswordEncoder(10) bcrypt.hash(..., 10) Different API, same algorithm and same security principle.
Password verification passwordEncoder.matches() await bcrypt.compare() In JavaScript the async call must be awaited.
Registration input Form parameters with validation annotations JSON DTO with class-validator decorators NestJS makes the request contract more explicit.
JWT creation Manual HMAC-SHA256 assembly jsonwebtoken.sign() Java reveals the internals; NestJS emphasizes practical application code.
Claims iss, aud, sub, scope, iat, exp sub, roles, expiration Claim shape is part of the contract with downstream services.
Access token lifetime 24 hours 15 minutes Shorter access tokens reduce exposure and pair well with refresh tokens.
Refresh token Model field exists, workflow not implemented Generated, stored, and used by refresh() The NestJS version currently has the more complete token lifecycle.
Error handling Central @RestControllerAdvice + ProblemDetail Nest built-in exceptions such as UnauthorizedException and ConflictException Both use framework-level HTTP exception handling.
API documentation Not included in this Java cut Swagger/OpenAPI decorators and generated docs The Node implementation currently has the stronger contract-documentation story.
Automated tests Not included in this Java cut Jest tests verify login and JWT claims Tests make the intended auth behavior executable.
Logging System.out.println() success events logAuthEvent(event, username) The Nest logger API intentionally gives callers no place to pass a password or token.
Round-by-round analysis

Who wins each round?

The point is not to crown a universally superior language. The point is to identify which implementation is stronger for the specific concern being discussed.

Round 1: Persistence

Java wins because it already has MongoDB persistence and a repository abstraction. The TypeScript version is still in-memory.

Edge: Java

Round 2: Password security

Both hash with bcrypt cost 10 and both compare submitted passwords against hashes rather than storing or comparing raw passwords.

Result: Tie

Round 3: JWT education

Java wins as a teaching implementation because students can see the token assembled from header, claims, encoding and signature.

Edge: Java

Round 4: API contract

TypeScript wins with JSON DTOs, runtime validation, field whitelisting and generated Swagger documentation.

Edge: TypeScript

Round 5: Token lifecycle

TypeScript wins because it implements both access and refresh tokens, plus a refresh operation that can issue a new access token.

Edge: TypeScript

Round 6: Testing

TypeScript wins because the supplied Jest suite verifies happy-path login, JWT claims and incorrect-password rejection.

Edge: TypeScript

Round 7: Error-response structure

Java has the more explicit centralized structure with ProblemDetail and several mapped exception categories.

Edge: Java

Round 8: Final weekly destination

The course goal is the Node/NestJS auth server, so TypeScript gets the symbolic belt even though both implementations remain valuable.

Edge: TypeScript
Code comparison

Same responsibilities, different syntax

These paired snippets let students compare the same concern side-by-side without getting lost in the full source files.

Java user model 
@Document("users")
public class UserAccount {
    @Id
    private String username;
    private String passwordHash;
    private String roles;
    private String refreshTokenHash;
    private String lineOfBusiness;
}
TypeScript user model 
interface StoredUser {
  passwordHash: string;
  roles: string[];
  refreshToken: string | null;
}

private readonly users =
  new Map<string, StoredUser>();
Java login 
public String login(
    String username,
    String password
) throws Exception {

    UserAccount user =
        users.findById(username).orElse(null);

    if (user == null ||
        !passwordEncoder.matches(
            password,
            user.getPasswordHash())) {

        throw new ResponseStatusException(
            HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED,
            "invalid username or password"
        );
    }

    return jwtService.issueAccessToken(
        username,
        user.getRoles()
    );
}
TypeScript login 
async login(
  username: string,
  password: string
): Promise<{
  accessToken: string;
  refreshToken: string;
}> {
  const user = this.users.get(username);

  const passwordMatches = user
    ? await bcrypt.compare(
        password,
        user.passwordHash
      )
    : false;

  if (!user || !passwordMatches) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      "invalid username or password"
    );
  }

  const accessToken =
    this.issueAccessToken(
      username,
      user.roles
    );

  const refreshToken =
    randomBytes(32).toString("hex");

  user.refreshToken = refreshToken;

  return {
    accessToken,
    refreshToken
  };
}
Java JWT creation 
claims.put("iss", "http://localhost:3000");
claims.put("aud", List.of("cartel-control"));
claims.put("sub", username);
claims.put("scope", roles);
claims.put("iat", Instant.now().getEpochSecond());
claims.put("exp",
    Instant.now().getEpochSecond() + 86400);

String unsigned =
    ENCODED_JWT_HEADER + "." +
    encodeJson(claims);

return unsigned + "." +
    signed(unsigned);
TypeScript JWT creation 
return jwt.sign(
  {
    sub: username,
    roles
  },
  JWT_SECRET,
  {
    algorithm: "HS256",
    expiresIn: "15m"
  }
);
Java controller input 
@PostMapping(
  value = "/login",
  consumes =
    MediaType.APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED_VALUE
)
public String login(
    @RequestParam
    @NotBlank
    @Size(min = 3, max = 50)
    String username,

    @RequestParam
    @NotBlank
    @Size(min = 3, max = 100)
    String password
) throws Exception {
    return authService.login(
        username,
        password
    );
}
NestJS controller input 
@Post("login")
@HttpCode(200)
@ApiOperation({
  summary:
    "Log in and receive an access token and a refresh token"
})
@ApiResponse({
  status: 200,
  description:
    "Login succeeded, tokens issued"
})
@ApiResponse({
  status: 401,
  description:
    "Invalid username or password"
})
login(@Body() body: LoginDto) {
  return this.authService.login(
    body.username,
    body.password
  );
}
NestJS runtime validation 
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    whitelist: true,
    forbidNonWhitelisted: true
  })
);
Jest verifies token claims 
it(
  "issues an access token that validates and carries the right claims",
  async () => {
    await service.register(
      "carol",
      "mission123",
      ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]
    );

    const { accessToken } =
      await service.login(
        "carol",
        "mission123"
      );

    const decoded =
      jwt.verify(
        accessToken,
        JWT_SECRET
      ) as jwt.JwtPayload;

    expect(decoded.sub)
      .toBe("carol");

    expect(decoded.roles)
      .toEqual(
        ["MISSION_OPERATOR"]
      );
  }
);

QUIZ ALERT: async bcrypt in JavaScript

bcrypt.compare() returns a Promise. The TypeScript implementation correctly uses await. If a student forgets the await, the Promise object itself is truthy and can accidentally make invalid credentials look successful.

Next round

What should students add to both implementations?

The best follow-up work is where the two stacks can be extended in parallel so students can see the same feature expressed twice.

Recommended extensions

  • Add user update and delete endpoints in both stacks.
  • Add a role-management endpoint that can grant or revoke roles from an existing user.
  • Finish the Java refresh-token workflow and store refresh-token hashes instead of raw tokens.
  • Move the TypeScript/NestJS implementation from the in-memory Map to a persistent database.
  • Add comparable automated tests and API docs to the Java implementation so the tooling comparison is more balanced.
Reveal the strongest classroom follow-up The best paired exercise is usually role management. Students add the same “grant role” capability to both services, then log in again and inspect how the newly issued JWT changes. That turns persistence, service logic, token issuance and authorization claims into one connected lesson.
